text: This course's closing lesson: one usable checklist pulling together all five chapters, built for reviewing a lineage record you're handed, or documenting one yourself from scratch. It isn't a trivia recap — every single line maps to a real failure mode you watched play out in this chapter's case studies, lessons 22 through 24.

Concepts, from Chapter One: the full path captured — origin, transformations, destination — with column-level detail wherever precision matters, since a table-level arrow alone hid Lesson 22's bug. Tracing, from Chapter Two: real source systems named specifically, logic captured precisely rather than vaguely as 'cleaning,' extended all the way to final consumption. Dependencies, from Chapter Three: every downstream consumer checked — recall Lesson 22's three affected reports — fragile upstream fields flagged, and a real source of record designated when systems overlap, recall Lesson 23's email match.

Documentation, from Chapter Four: findable by someone other than the builder, with an actual plan for keeping it current — who updates it, and when. Applied practice, from Chapter Five: when something breaks, walk the lineage path backward from the broken figure, the way Lesson 24 did, instead of re-checking every system from scratch — and after any fix, update the record itself, not just the code.

Every case study in this course shared the same shape: a number or a record looked fine for a long time, until one upstream change quietly broke an assumption nobody had written down. The single habit that catches each one earlier — call it the impact-first habit — is always the same: when something upstream changes, check what's downstream before assuming it's fine. That's exactly what impact analysis from Chapter Three, and column-level lineage from Chapter One, exist to make fast enough to actually do every time.

That closes all five chapters and twenty-five lessons of Data Lineage and Impact Analysis — from what lineage is, to tracing it through real systems, to using it for impact analysis, documenting it, and applying it to realistic scenarios. The Data Governance path continues next with Master and Reference Data Management: deciding, for the handful of concepts every system depends on, which one gets to be the authoritative version everything else defers to. If Lesson 23's missing source-of-record decision stood out to you, the next course solves that problem.
